title: Founded Ford Motor Company in Detroit
statement: Founded Ford Motor Company in Detroit on June 16, 1903, with twelve investors and $28,000 in capital after two prior unsuccessful attempts at automobile manufacturing.
outcome: The company took its first order on July 15, 1903, an $850 Model A from Chicago dentist Ernst Pfenning, and within five years introduced the Model T.

title: Launched the Model T as a car for the great multitude
statement: Launched the Model T on October 1, 1908, as a low-priced automobile engineered for ordinary Americans rather than for the wealthy few.
outcome: Approximately 15 million Model Ts were built by May 26, 1927; the Model T is generally regarded as the first mass-affordable automobile and the template for every low-cost car program that followed.

title: Built the moving assembly line at Highland Park
statement: Built the moving assembly line at the Highland Park plant in 1913 after experiments with a movable line for assembling flywheel magnetos, collapsing the time required to build a Model T to roughly ninety minutes.
outcome: The assembly line created a labor-turnover crisis that directly triggered the $5 workday of January 1914, and became the template Henry Ford exported to the world.

title: Announced the five-dollar day as profit-sharing
statement: Announced on January 5, 1914, with vice president James Couzens, that Ford Motor Company would roughly double its workers' wages to five dollars a day as a profit-sharing payment.
outcome: Mechanics from across the country flooded Detroit chasing the new wage, labor turnover collapsed, and the bet was widely credited with turning Ford's own payroll into a captive customer base for the Model T.

title: Published antisemitic Dearborn Independent and apologized
statement: Published The Dearborn Independent from 1919 through 1927, including the antisemitic 'International Jew' series that began in 1920 and bound some five hundred thousand copies distributed through Ford dealerships.
outcome: On June 30, 1927, Ford released a signed letter of apology after a libel suit by Aaron Sapiro; the last issue of the Independent was published in December 1927. The underlying pamphlets continued to circulate abroad for decades.
